survey.provenance: INTERPRETATION — descriptions written by this archive from the transcript. Not a record of what was said. No dialogue is reproduced.
survey.why: The film's dialogue is not published, because a full transcript is the documentary's script in substance. A scene guide gives a reader the film's content and shape without reproducing the work.

scenes.title: Brazzaville, ten years later
scenes.description: Opens in the Congo. He is travelling with a small group and says he has not been back in a decade. He describes the country as changed, the government as corrupt, and — unusually for an opening — admits the group itself is fracturing after only three days.

scenes.title: The chant
scenes.description: A rhythmic, deliberately crude chant sequence, cut as a musical interlude rather than narration. It sets the film's register early: comic, aggressive, and unwilling to present him as respectable.

scenes.title: Who the work is for
scenes.description: His clearest statement of intent: he makes art for people who do not care about art, do not visit museums, and would not claim to appreciate it.

scenes.title: Meeting a collaborator at Comic Con
scenes.description: How a young artist approached him at Comic Con wanting to contribute to his magazine, and how little he thought of the pitch at the time.

scenes.title: Graffiti, without the gang
scenes.description: He separates himself from the gang culture around writing. He was in it for the drawing, not the territory — putting Bible verses and jokes on walls rather than repeating his own name for status.

scenes.title: Being lied to
scenes.description: The film's account of his motive: adults telling him what to do and giving him misleading instructions. Shoplifting, graffiti and gambling arrive as the answer to that, not as thrill-seeking.

scenes.title: The gorilla in the tree
scenes.description: Back in the Congo. He spots something far off in a tree, photographs it to zoom in, and realises it is a gorilla — which then climbs down toward the group.

scenes.title: The warden's speech
scenes.description: A juvenile lock-up as a boy. A warden comes out in the middle of the night to frighten the group with what happens to children in jail, and it works.

scenes.title: The storefront
scenes.description: A riot scene: the crowd cannot get through the security mesh until a man steps out and shoots the lock off, at which point everyone goes in.

scenes.title: Two and a half years
scenes.description: How long the stealing went on, and the scale of the police response on the night it ended — which he found funnier than frightening.

scenes.title: The letter to the magazines
scenes.description: He notices adult magazines use as much illustration as mainstream ones, with the lowest standards and the highest rates, and writes in. It is the film's turn from crime toward paid work.

scenes.title: The ice cream shop wall
scenes.description: He criticises the art on a shop's walls out loud, is overheard by the owner, and the complaint turns into a commission.

scenes.title: Handing over the wall
scenes.description: He gives other painters walls and tells them to paint whatever they want. The film uses it to show a man who has been given nothing and now hands out opportunities.

scenes.title: Twelve months, twelve women
scenes.description: A work built around a woman for each month of the year, and the reaction to a young artist celebrating promiscuity that openly.

scenes.title: The replies
scenes.description: Responses to that work read aloud — hostile, obscene, occasionally admiring. The film lets them run without defending him.

scenes.title: Two weeks before Christmas
scenes.description: A foot chase ending in arrest on a shopping street, with couples and shoppers watching. One of the film's sharpest scenes of public shame.

scenes.title: Jail food, and natto
scenes.description: Inside: the rationed peaches, the milk carton with no straw. Cut against him enthusing about natto, the fermented beans he eats by choice.

scenes.title: The friend he lost
scenes.description: A quieter passage about an estrangement he cannot fully explain and describes as simply sad.

scenes.title: Caught for a lifetime
scenes.description: He argues he was arrested for something trivial but sentenced, in effect, for everything he had done before it — and that had they let him go he would have taken revenge.

scenes.title: The grandmother's Jesus
scenes.description: A drawing from his grandmother: an image of Jesus rendered entirely out of the words of the Old Testament, which he keeps close.

scenes.title: Japan
scenes.description: Others describe how difficult his recent work has become to read, and connect it to his imprisonment in Japan and to a way of processing it they find unfamiliar.

scenes.title: After the sentence
scenes.description: His career accelerates immediately after release — so much work that he never has to stop and think about what happened.

scenes.title: The meter
scenes.description: He describes an internal clock he believes is running out, and thinks it explains why he never slows down, even on commercial jobs.

scenes.title: Ruining it on purpose
scenes.description: Three days of careful rendering destroyed by a single deliberate stroke. He treats the impulse as involuntary rather than as a decision.

scenes.title: Understand it or don't
scenes.description: An argument about being taken as he is. He asks to be accepted as an artist and is impatient with anyone wanting the benefits without that.

scenes.title: More options than ever
scenes.description: He pushes back on the reading of his life as tragic, and asks why the same facts cannot be read as freedom.

scenes.title: The office
scenes.description: Painting a workspace people will sit in every day, in colour dense enough that he calls it distracting — and likes it for that.

scenes.title: Finding God, losing him
scenes.description: He says he has found God and lost him about five times, and asks how many times a person is expected to do that.

scenes.title: Being out is the hard part
scenes.description: The film's flattest, least defended moment: the shows, the sales and the freedom do not deliver what he expected, and the relief keeps passing.

scenes.title: The whale
scenes.description: He explains the name of the whale in his work — taken from a word he learned from a girlfriend in college — and the film lets the joke stand as the ending it deserves.

scenes.title: Party
scenes.description: Closes mid-party, with the questions unanswered.
